Downloaded this with high hopes after a masterpiece like Hollow Knight. At first, I was thrilled to rediscover that familiar hand-crafted atmosphere. The map, dialogues, and atmosphere lived up to the first game. But then the boss fights started.

Finding that satisfying character progression and power curve from Hollow Knight is quite difficult in Silksong. After a point, I started playing just so it would end and I could uninstall it. Unnecessarily over-difficult bosses and the constant spawning of secondary minions turn the boss fights away from the sweet, familiar challenge we knew. Instead, they transform into a Dark Souls 3-style finger-exercise that tests your stress levels and drains the joy out of playing.

After a while, you realize that the charm system from the old game is very weak here. No matter how brilliantly you explore, strengthening your character requires a much more detailed and grueling exploration, and it doesn't unfold naturally alongside the story like it did in the first game. (And I'm a player who combs through every inch of the map.)

I’ve already put over 30 hours into the game and I have no idea how much is left, but this is the first time I’m struggling this hard not to uninstall a game before finishing it.

Hollow Knight is a masterpiece, Silksong is just miserable. It's not the difficulty, it's the tone. Everything is more grotesque, baroque and overwrought than the last game, from art to story, NPCs and biomes have all had a significant charisma downgrade, to the point where I no longer care about exploring, because every area is just another boring slog with little sense of wonder or mystery. HK had a big infusion of the Studio Ghibli magic, and that's almost all gone in this sequel. I have never put so much time into a game I enjoyed so little.

What's left is a masochistic slog, with a downgraded gamefeel in the character to increase the difficulty of  combat. While Hornet is technically more mobile, the jump and basic attack have been mildly nerfed which means more precise timing and movement are required for all things. The game is harder and just feels noticeably worse than HK for the minute to minute gameplay, like a shoe that just slightly doesn't fit. Is the justification for this significantly more interesting challengers? 

Not really. While the behavior of the enemies has been made far more complex, which seems better at first, it's still not really interesting most of the time. The largest issue is that the more complex attach options for the enemies often results in awkward pairings of enemies. Two enemies attacking at the same time and being able to pass through each other with semi complicated attack options often leads to situations where avoiding one attack simply means you will almost definitely take contact damage from the other (the damage type that makes you feel stupid). There's no way to strategically deal with both at the same time, so most often you just try to aggro one away and deal with them individually, reducing the complexity of every fight as much as your can, but even with the multiple attacks many enemies now have, few are particularly interesting one on one. Hollow Knights comparably simple enemies were often full easy 1 on 1, but could create interesting dynamics when paired together or with environmental challenges. 

Speaking of environmental challenges, the main one in every biome is that you are on the ground and most of the enemies can fly. They all hover just barely in reach of a single swing at the height of your jump, and some will dodge away when possible. Will a single swing kill them or change their behavior? No, they'll be a slog, you'll need to jump and hit them multiple times, constantly, in almost every biome, throughout the entire game. And remember, jumping and attacking feel fundamentally less satisfying than in HK, and the risk of contact damage and feeling stupid are way higher. It just makes you wish you had a gun to shoot them out of the air, and when I got a tool that basically let's you delete more basic flyers, I realized how little I enjoyed engaging with any of them, and they are all over every biome, cluttering up boss runbacks, just being a pebble in a shoe that doesn't quite fit for almost every step you'll take. And their placement is consistently in places that mean you have to stop to deal with them, no matter how boring and difficult it is. Difficult because it will always require some level of coordination, but boring because it's the exact same behavior and strategy for almost all of the flying enemies. Hard and boring is a rough sell for something I'm choosing to do with my free time. Some enemy placements feel like the are suggestive of an almost "Lisa" like contempt for the player. 

People have made a lot of the difficulty and stingy economy, and while those are issues, the bigger issue to me is still the tone. Pharloom and the Citadel are both just miserable places that I don't enjoy traversing, in pursuit of a story I don't care about. I kept pushing forward hoping for bit of the Hollow Knight magic to start to sparkle again, but at 60 hours with enemies I hate dealing with, uninspiring NPCs and environments, and all of that on top of an incredibly punishing difficulty, I just don't care enough to push any further.  While it's an insane amount of content for 20 bucks, and a ton of hard work and care have clearly gone into it, I can only say that I just didn't really enjoy almost any of my time with this game.

[h1]Harsh, but not fair[/h1]

Hollow Knight was harsh but fair. Silksong is harsh and nothing else, and that difference is the whole of my complaint.

I knew what I was buying. Nobody picks up a Team Cherry Metroidvania expecting a gentle stroll. I accept the beating. What I don't accept is a beating handed out by a referee who has quietly left the building. I'm about halfway through and going for 100%, so treat this as a report from the trenches, not the summit.

[h2]The arithmetic of suffering[/h2]
Ordinary enemies hit for two masks. Not bosses, not armored brutes, but things that look like mice. Meanwhile early mice, frogs and birds take around four needle hits each, which is what genuinely dangerous enemies took in Hollow Knight. The needle upgrade arrives deep into Act One, so your damage stays stunted for hours. You hit like a wet noodle, and the noodle is fighting rodents in plate armor.

[h2]A hoarder's economy of silk[/h2]
Bind heals three masks, even midair. But when everything hits for two, you're never actually back on your feet. So you hoard silk, and the counter, needle throw and the rest of Hornet's kit sit unused. A toolkit you're afraid to use is a display case. Some stretches practically require you to cheese enemies for silk, stepping in and out of a room until the meter is full. I never once had to farm soul in Hollow Knight.

[h2]Benches, runbacks and trap benches[/h2]
In Hollow Knight, a bench ahead meant trouble was coming, and the Dreamgate covered the few brutal runbacks. Silksong has neither mercy. Benches sit far from where you die. In Sinner's Road there's a bench you have to repair by crossing a deadly gauntlet, and if you die the nearest bench is back in Greymoor. Twice I found trap benches that kill you for sitting down. Hollow Knight never pulled anything like that. A bench there was a promise of safety. Here it's a punchline.

[h2]The bosses are fine. Getting to them is not.[/h2]
The bosses are hard, about regular-Grimm hard across the board, but none I've faced has been unfair. What ruins them is the runback: a platforming section you have to clear without taking a hit, because one lost mask can decide the fight. Then a five-to-six-minute boss fight, death, and the walk again. That's not a challenge. It's a humiliation ritual. And no, runbacks don't need to "train" me. The rest of the game can do that.

[h2]Poverty as a design pillar[/h2]
Everything costs rosaries and you're always broke. In Hollow Knight, being broke was your own fault. In Silksong it's a toll booth on every road.

[h2]Sadism, itemized[/h2]
Platforming that wants near frame-perfect play. Enemies parked in your jump path so you have to eat the hit. Mount Fay's falling pillars, which you have to touch to make solid ground, with zero hint from the game. And Bilewater, which earns every bit of its reputation. I'm a player who never uses exploits or god mode, and I've had to look up guides and YouTube videos to get through sections of this game.

[h2]Pain without payoff[/h2]
Yes, Hollow Knight had the Path of Pain and the 15,000 Geo Unbreakable Strength. But that suffering was rare, optional, and paid off with a cutscene and arguably the best charm in the game. Silksong is full of mini Paths of Pain that reward you with a flea, a rosary, or some craft metal. Hollow Knight charged a lot for something great. Silksong charges a lot for pocket change.

[h2]A confession, without honor[/h2]
When I sense death coming, I now pause, quit and reload so I wake up at a bench instead of chasing my cocoon over lava or spikes. I'm not proud of it. Worse, plenty of YouTube guides from regular players tell you to save-quit at the end of long sections just to skip the walk back. In Hollow Knight, the end of a long trek gave you a shortcut. When the community's best practice is stepping outside the game to skip the game, something is wrong.

[h2]To the "get good" crowd[/h2]
Hornet being "tactical" doesn't explain why a frog needs four stabs, and "it's a different world" doesn't explain an economy built to keep you broke. Those are excuses for tuning. "Get good" isn't a rebuttal, it's declining to have the argument.

[h2]Credit where it's due[/h2]
Silksong is gorgeous, the soundtrack is incredible, the bosses are memorable, the story is good, the world feels more alive than Hallownest, and it's genuinely funny. Those things, plus my own stubbornness, are why I'm still playing. The machinery underneath is the problem.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]
Difficulty is a contract: the game gets to be hard, and you get a fair shot at winning. Hollow Knight honored it. Silksong keeps the first half.

Hollow Knight was a hike up a mountain. Hard, beautiful, and people say "I might try that someday" when you tell them. Silksong is walking barefoot on hot coals with no camera rolling, and people just ask why you'd do that.

[b]Hollow Knight I finished out of love. Silksong I'm finishing out of spite.[/b]
